items.why: The explicit negation distinguishes what Jeroboam fails to do from what he does again.
The answer is recoverable, but the question’s two uses of “he” make it awkwardly ambiguous.
It cleanly distinguishes the collective summary from Jonathan’s defeat of one descendant.
The officer is the clear antecedent, and the competitor is a plausible role reversal.
The action sequence clearly separates the old prophet from the sons who saddle the donkey.
The first and second covenants provide a precise, strongly discriminating contrast.
The chronology directly places Jotham’s succession after Uzziah’s burial.
The stated reason is the Lord’s affliction, though the priests’ simultaneous action creates some causal competition.
The quoted plan clearly places entering the city after capturing the people, despite awkward wording.
The men explicitly reject entering the city and decide to surrender at the Aramean camp.
The ordered account clearly identifies Sibbekai as the first killer at Gob.
“The news” is a vague answer that tests little beyond a nearby generic noun.
The command “Seize him” clearly targets the man of God rather than the speaking king.
The passage directly states that Azariah and the priests followed Uzziah into the temple.
The today-versus-tomorrow contrast is explicit and highly discriminating.
Zechariah is explicitly identified as Uzziah’s instructor in the fear of God.
The reply to the officer’s doubt is clearly the prediction that he will see but not eat.
The refusal is explicitly grounded in the Lord’s command, not the size of the offer.
The immediate sequence clearly places Paul’s continued talking directly before his departure.
The narrative order clearly puts mobilizing the army before laying siege.
Jehoiada is the explicit giver, while David is only the weapons’ former owner.
The order explicitly concerns the accusers presenting their case to the addressee.
The purpose is explicit, though “take Amaziah’s son” is a slightly unnatural formulation.
The passage clearly places the 307,500 men under the 2,600 family leaders’ command.
The man of God is the clear traveler killed by the lion, not the prophet who saddled the donkey.
The officer assigned to the gate is explicitly trampled there, clearly excluding the king.
The two off-duty companies receive the specific instruction to guard the temple for the king.
The letter heading unambiguously separates its writer, Claudius Lysias, from its recipient.
Abishai explicitly kills Ishbi-Benob while rescuing David, making the role contrast strong.
After recognizing their wrongdoing, the men explicitly resolve to report immediately to the palace.
Paul’s quoted words clearly identify the young man as the one with information.
The messengers’ return and report immediately precede the people’s plundering.
The final clause clearly attributes love of the soil to Uzziah, though the question is somewhat awkward.
The speaker explicitly says that her own son was cooked and eaten first.
The man of God explicitly intercedes after the king asks him to pray.
The passage provides a complete three-group list and clearly contrasts it with the tribute-paying Ammonites.
The body is taken first to the prophet’s city and only afterward placed in his tomb.
Joash is clearly the child hidden with his nurse for six years.
The passage explicitly links the city’s calm to Athaliah’s death, not merely to the rejoicing.
The commander addresses the two centurions, who must prepare the listed detachment.
The Arameans explicitly imagine the Hittite and Egyptian kings coming to attack them.
“This murderer” refers to the messenger’s master, the king, though the antecedent requires inference.
Within the old prophet’s claimed message, “him” clearly refers to the man of God.
Paul’s intended departure the next day is explicitly given as the reason for speaking so long.
The soldiers return after allowing the cavalry to continue with Paul.
The plural victims who flee naked and bleeding are clearly Sceva’s seven sons.
The intended distinction is present, but “on the items’ arrival” is unnatural and not stated.
The conspirators explicitly ask the council to petition the commander to bring Paul.
The practitioners burn the scrolls immediately after bringing them together, before calculating their value.
The explicit sword order targets anyone following Athaliah, but she is also subsequently executed, weakening the contrast.
Hearing the guards’ and people’s noise explicitly prompts Athaliah to go to the crowd.
The ambushers are said to await consent, but Paul’s resulting transfer is also a practical prerequisite.
The warning is directly addressed to the man of God from Judah, not the old prophet delivering it.
The prophecy explicitly names Josiah as the one who will sacrifice the high-place priests.
